title: Manhattan Incident and Silent Coup Consolidate Army Rule
description: In June 1951 naval officers seized Prime Minister Phibun aboard a US dredge, the Manhattan; army and air force units bombed the vessel until Phibun escaped by swimming ashore. The navy's political power was fatally weakened. In November, Phibun staged a self-coup abolishing the 1949 constitution and reinstating an older authoritarian charter, entrenching army supremacy.

title: Anti-Communist Activities Act Criminalises Dissent
description: Thailand enacted the Anti-Communist Activities Act in 1952, criminalising membership in or support of communist organisations. The law was applied broadly to suppress labour activists, political dissidents, and ethnic Chinese residents suspected of Maoist sympathies. It established a precedent of using national-security legislation to curtail civil liberties that recurred in subsequent decades.

title: Thailand Signs Manila Pact, Joins SEATO as Founding Member
description: Thailand was a founding signatory of the Southeast Asia Collective Defence Treaty signed in Manila in September 1954, establishing SEATO. The alliance provided Bangkok with a formal American security commitment against communist aggression in Indochina. Thailand positioned itself as a frontline Cold War state, gaining substantial US military and economic assistance in return.

title: Sarit Thanarat Coup Ousts Phibun, Inaugurates Military Developmental State
description: Field Marshal Sarit Thanarat staged a coup on 16 September 1957, ousting Prime Minister Phibun after flawed elections and accusations of corruption. Sarit then staged a second coup in October 1958, abolishing the constitution and governing by revolutionary decree. His rule concentrated power in the military while directing development resources into infrastructure and industrial planning.

title: First National Economic Development Plan Launched with World Bank
description: Thailand launched its First National Economic Development Plan (1961-1966) in 1959 with guidance from World Bank economists, prioritising road construction, power generation, and agricultural productivity. The National Economic and Social Development Board (NESDB) was created to coordinate planning. American development assistance and Japanese reparations provided much of the capital, integrating Thailand into Cold War development networks.

title: Southern Malay-Muslim Insurgency Begins in Border Provinces
description: Low-level insurgency by Malay-Muslim separatist groups intensified in the southern border provinces of Pattani, Yala, and Narathiwat in the early 1960s, driven by Thai assimilationist policies and suppression of Malay language and culture. The state's alienation of the Muslim-majority region created a grievance-driven conflict that persisted with periodic flare-ups for more than six decades.

title: Communist Party of Thailand Launches Armed Insurgency
description: The Communist Party of Thailand (CPT) formally launched armed insurgency in the rural northeast in 1961, drawing on Maoist tactics and Chinese material support. The insurgency reflected deep grievances among impoverished northeasterners excluded from urban development gains. The military responded with combined counterinsurgency and rural development programmes.

title: Thanat-Rusk Communique Formalises Bilateral US Security Pledge
description: In March 1962, Thai Foreign Minister Thanat Khoman and US Secretary of State Dean Rusk issued a joint statement affirming that the United States would defend Thailand unilaterally, without requiring collective SEATO agreement. The bilateral pledge strengthened Thailand's security position as communist pressure intensified in Laos and Vietnam. It became the cornerstone of the US-Thai alliance throughout the Vietnam War era.

title: Thai Troops Deployed to Vietnam — Queen's Cobras Commit to US War
description: Thailand sent troops to South Vietnam beginning in 1965, eventually committing around 11,000 soldiers known as the Queen's Cobras at peak deployment. Thai participation earned significant US financial compensation and military equipment transfers. The deployment aligned Thailand firmly with the American war effort and reinforced its status as a frontline Cold War ally.

title: Bangkok Declaration Establishes ASEAN with Thailand as Co-Founder
description: The Association of Southeast Asian Nations was formally created with the signing of the Bangkok Declaration on 8 August 1967, uniting Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Singapore. Thai Foreign Minister Thanat Khoman played an instrumental role in crafting the organisation's founding principles of non-interference and peaceful cooperation. ASEAN bore Bangkok's name as the host city, reflecting Thailand's central diplomatic role.

title: New Constitution Restores Partial Civilian Government Under Thanom
description: The Thanom government promulgated a new constitution in 1968 restoring a bicameral parliament, though an appointed Senate preserved military dominance. Elections in 1969 produced a partial civilian government with Thanom remaining as prime minister. The constitutional experiment reflected international pressure but real power stayed with the military triumvirate of Thanom, Praphas, and Narong.

title: Thanom Self-Coup Abolishes Constitution and Bans Political Parties
description: Prime Minister Thanom Kittikachorn staged a self-coup in November 1971, annulling the 1968 constitution, dissolving parliament, and banning all political parties. The Thanom-Praphas-Narong triumvirate ruled through a National Executive Council wielding combined legislative and executive authority. The coup reflected the military's discomfort with even the partial democratisation of the late 1960s.

title: October 14 Uprising Topples Military Triumvirate
description: On 14 October 1973, massive student-led protests in Bangkok — swelling to over 400,000 — toppled the Thanom-Praphas-Narong military triumvirate after troops fired on demonstrators, killing at least 77. King Bhumibol intervened decisively, granting audience to student leaders and facilitating the military leaders' departure from Thailand. The uprising is celebrated as Thailand's first successful democratic revolution and ushered in a brief democratic period.

title: People's Constitution Promulgated — Most Liberal Charter in Thai History
description: Thailand promulgated a new democratic constitution in October 1974, drafted by a constituent assembly and providing for a fully elected parliament and extensive civil liberties. Multiple political parties formed rapidly and a vibrant free press emerged. The charter represented the most liberal constitutional framework in Thai history to that point and set the stage for the 1975 elections.

title: Thailand Normalises Relations with China, Ending Decades of Isolation
description: Prime Minister Kukrit Pramoj visited Beijing in July 1975 and established full diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China, ending Thailand's decades-long alignment with Taipei. The normalisation followed communist victories in Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos, making continued isolation of Beijing strategically untenable. China's subsequent willingness to end material support for the CPT facilitated the insurgency's eventual collapse.

title: Communist Indochina Victories Create Domino Alarm in Bangkok
description: The fall of Saigon and Phnom Penh in April 1975 and the Pathet Lao takeover of Laos in December created acute strategic anxiety in Bangkok about communist expansion. Thousands of Thai students and leftists, fearing a right-wing crackdown, fled to the jungle to join the CPT. Thailand accelerated its diplomacy with China while pressing the United States not to abandon the region.

title: October 6 Massacre and Military Coup End Democratic Experiment
description: On 6 October 1976, rightwing paramilitaries and police attacked students at Thammasat University, killing at least 46 with unofficial estimates exceeding 100. Hours later the military staged a coup, abolished the constitution, and installed an ultra-royalist government, ending Thailand's brief democratic period. The massacre traumatised a generation and drove thousands of students and intellectuals into CPT insurgency camps.

title: Vietnam Invades Cambodia, Creating Security Crisis on Thailand's Border
description: Vietnam's invasion of Cambodia in December 1978 and subsequent occupation created a major security crisis on Thailand's northeastern border. Bangkok hosted hundreds of thousands of Cambodian refugees while coordinating covertly with China and the United States to support Khmer resistance factions. Thailand became a frontline state in a new Cold War confrontation that shaped its foreign and security policy throughout the 1980s.

title: General Prem Tinsulanonda Takes Power — Eight Years of Semi-Democracy
description: General Prem Tinsulanonda assumed the premiership in February 1980 after Kriangsak resigned amid economic difficulties. Prem's government, lasting until 1988, established stable semi-democracy in which the military set strategic parameters while civilians managed the economy. His close relationship with King Bhumibol gave him unique cross-institutional authority and helped him survive two coup attempts.

title: CPT Insurgency Collapses Under Amnesty Policy and Chinese Withdrawal
description: Prime Minister Prem's amnesty for CPT fighters, combined with China ending its support for the movement after the Sino-Vietnamese rupture, accelerated the insurgency's collapse. By the early 1980s thousands of student radicals surrendered and returned to civilian life, many becoming prominent academics and civil society figures. Thailand's two-decade communist insurgency was effectively over by 1983.

title: Young Turks Coup Attempt Fails After Royal Endorsement of Prem
description: In April 1981, a faction of military officers known as the Young Turks attempted a coup against the Prem government. Prem and key cabinet members fled to Nakhon Ratchasima with King Bhumibol, and the king's broadcast support for Prem caused the coup to collapse within days. The episode demonstrated the decisive political weight of royal endorsement in Thai civil-military relations.

title: Baht Devaluation Corrects Trade Deficit, Sets Stage for Export Boom
description: Thailand devalued the baht in 1984 to address a widening trade deficit and improve export competitiveness. The adjustment, managed by technocratic central bankers, stabilised the economy and set the stage for an export-led manufacturing boom in the late 1980s. Sound macroeconomic management became a hallmark of the Prem era and attracted foreign investment.

title: Plaza Accord Triggers Wave of Japanese Manufacturing Investment
description: The 1985 Plaza Accord's sharp yen appreciation prompted Japanese manufacturers to relocate production to lower-cost countries, with Thailand receiving a major share. Electronics, automotive parts, and textile factories multiplied on Thailand's eastern seaboard. The investment influx transformed Thailand from a predominantly agricultural exporter into a manufacturing powerhouse over the following decade.

title: Chatichai Wins Election — First Elected PM in Over a Decade
description: General Chatichai Choonhavan led his Chart Thai party to parliamentary victory in July 1988, becoming Thailand's first elected prime minister in more than a decade. Chatichai pledged to turn Indochina from a battlefield into a marketplace, pursuing economic engagement with Vietnam and Cambodia. His government oversaw rapid economic growth exceeding 10 percent annually but was also associated with extensive ministerial corruption.

title: Economic Boom Reaches Tiger Economy Levels
description: Thailand's GDP grew at over 10 percent annually in 1988-1989, earning comparisons to the East Asian tiger economies. Manufacturing exports surged, foreign direct investment reached record levels, and Bangkok underwent rapid physical transformation. The boom created a new urban middle class with rising political expectations that would fuel demands for accountable governance.

title: Military Coup Ousts Chatichai on Corruption Grounds
description: On 23 February 1991 the Supreme Command staged a coup against Prime Minister Chatichai, accusing his government of unprecedented corruption and parliamentary dictatorship. The National Peace-Keeping Council junta appointed respected diplomat Anand Panyarachun as interim prime minister and oversaw drafting of a new constitution. The coup was initially accepted by many Bangkokians exhausted by ministerial venality.

title: Black May Massacre Triggers King's Intervention and Democratic Restoration
description: Mass protests against unelected Prime Minister Suchinda Kraprayoon in May 1992 were met with lethal military force, killing an estimated 52-100 demonstrators in what became known as Black May. King Bhumibol summoned both Suchinda and protest leader Chamlong before cameras on 20 May, demanding an end to the confrontation; Suchinda resigned four days later. New elections in September 1992 produced a Democrat-led civilian government under Chuan Leekpai.

title: Thailand's 100 Percent Condom Programme Becomes Global AIDS Model
description: Thailand gained international recognition for its 100 Percent Condom Programme, which dramatically reduced HIV transmission rates in commercial sex settings through frank public health communication and mandatory condom use. The programme demonstrated that behavioural interventions could curb an epidemic in a conservative society. By the mid-1990s Thailand's AIDS response was cited as one of Asia's most effective.

title: BIBF Capital Account Liberalisation Creates Structural Currency Mismatch
description: Thailand established the Bangkok International Banking Facility (BIBF) in 1993-1994, allowing Thai banks to borrow cheaply offshore and on-lend domestically. The facility created a structural currency mismatch as banks borrowed in dollars and yen to fund baht-denominated loans to real estate and equity speculators. This vulnerability would prove catastrophic in the 1997 financial crisis.

title: Baht Collapse Triggers Asian Financial Crisis
description: On 2 July 1997 the Thai government abandoned the baht's peg to the US dollar, triggering a collapse that spread rapidly across Southeast and East Asia. The baht lost nearly 60 percent of its value within months, devastating businesses with unhedged dollar debts and producing a severe recession with GDP contracting approximately 10 percent in 1998. The crisis exposed the fragility of Thailand's credit-fuelled development model.

title: IMF Rescue Package — $17.2 Billion with Austerity Conditions
description: Thailand accepted an IMF rescue package of approximately $17.2 billion in August 1997, the first major Asian economy to do so, requiring fiscal austerity, financial sector restructuring, and closure of 58 finance companies. The IMF conditions were deeply unpopular and the resulting recession caused mass unemployment and rising poverty. The episode fundamentally shaped Thai attitudes toward international financial institutions.

title: People's Constitution — Most Democratic Charter in Thai History
description: Amid the economic crisis, Thailand promulgated a landmark new constitution in October 1997, drafted by a directly elected constituent assembly. The so-called People's Constitution introduced a directly elected Senate, an independent Constitutional Court, an electoral commission, and anti-corruption bodies. It was the most participatory constitution in Thai history, designed to reduce vote-buying and clientelism.

title: Thaksin Shinawatra Founds Thai Rak Thai, Reshaping Electoral Politics
description: Telecommunications billionaire Thaksin Shinawatra founded the Thai Rak Thai (Thais Love Thais) party in 1998-1999, positioning it as a populist force offering concrete economic programmes to rural voters. Thaksin's business resources and media ownership enabled an unprecedented national political machine combining populism and technocratic policy. His party represented a new style in Thai politics oriented toward the rural north and northeast.

title: Thaksin Wins Landslide — Thai Rak Thai Takes 248 Seats
description: Thaksin Shinawatra led Thai Rak Thai to a landslide victory in the January 2001 election, winning 248 of 500 seats and forming a dominant majority government. His campaign's 30-baht universal healthcare scheme and village fund promises electrified rural voters who felt left behind by the metropolitan-centred Democrat Party. The election marked a tectonic shift toward explicit rural populist mobilisation.

title: 30-Baht Universal Healthcare Scheme Launched
description: Prime Minister Thaksin introduced the 30-baht universal healthcare scheme in 2001-2002, providing basic medical care to every Thai for a nominal co-payment. The policy dramatically expanded healthcare access for the rural poor and became Thaksin's most popular programme. It demonstrated how targeted social policy could build durable political loyalty among previously marginalised constituencies.

title: War on Drugs — Over 2,500 Extrajudicial Killings in 90 Days
description: Prime Minister Thaksin launched a war on drugs in February 2003, and more than 2,500 people were killed in ninety days in circumstances suggesting extrajudicial execution, with many deaths uninvestigated. Human rights organisations condemned the campaign as state-sanctioned murder, while Thaksin's supporters credited it with reducing drug availability. The episode raised profound questions about rule of law under elected government.

title: Southern Insurgency Escalates — Krue Se Mosque and Tak Bai Incidents
description: Islamist militant violence in the southern border provinces escalated sharply from January 2004. In April, security forces stormed the historic Krue Se Mosque killing 32 militants. In October the Tak Bai incident saw 85 detainees die of suffocation during transport in overcrowded military trucks. Both events drew international condemnation and deepened Muslim alienation in Pattani, Yala, and Narathiwat.

title: Indian Ocean Tsunami Kills 5,400 on Thailand's Andaman Coast
description: The catastrophic Indian Ocean tsunami of 26 December 2004 struck Thailand's Andaman Sea coast, killing approximately 5,400 people including thousands of foreign tourists at Khao Lak, Phi Phi Island, and Phuket. Khao Lak alone suffered nearly 4,000 confirmed deaths. The disaster prompted unprecedented international emergency response and demonstrated the vulnerability of Thailand's coastal tourism infrastructure.

title: Thaksin Wins Unprecedented Outright Parliamentary Majority
description: Thai Rak Thai won 377 of 500 seats in the February 2005 election, the first time in Thai history that a single party achieved an outright majority. The result reflected Thaksin's dominance among rural voters in the north and northeast and made him the most electorally powerful politician in Thai history. However, the Yellow Shirt opposition movement emerged in the same year, launching a new cycle of political polarisation.

title: Shin Corp Sale and Yellow Shirts Trigger September 19 Military Coup
description: Thaksin's family's tax-free sale of their Shin Corporation stake to Singapore's Temasek for 73 billion baht in January 2006 ignited Yellow Shirt protests that destabilised his government. On 19 September 2006, while Thaksin was at the UN in New York, the military staged a bloodless coup, abolishing the constitution and dissolving the Constitutional Court. Thaksin went into exile, ending the most dominant electoral project in Thai history.

title: Military-Drafted Constitution Approved in Restricted Referendum
description: A military-drafted constitution was approved in a referendum in August 2007 with 57 percent support, amid restrictions on campaigning against it and arrests of critics. The 2007 charter contained provisions limiting the power of future elected governments through unelected bodies and independent agencies. Critics characterised it as an anti-Thaksin constitution designed to prevent his allies from governing effectively.

title: Yellow Shirts Occupy Airports; Constitutional Court Dissolves Pro-Thaksin Parties
description: The People's Alliance for Democracy occupied Suvarnabhumi and Don Mueang airports in November 2008, stranding hundreds of thousands of passengers for eight days. The Constitutional Court then dissolved the People's Power Party and two coalition partners in December, engineering a coalition change that brought Democrat leader Abhisit Vejjajiva to power without an election. The events deepened perceptions that judicial and extra-parliamentary means were used to override electoral outcomes.

title: Global Financial Crisis Contracts Thai Economy
description: Thailand's export-dependent economy contracted approximately 2.3 percent in 2009 amid the global financial crisis, with manufacturing and tourism hit by the collapse in external demand. The government's fiscal stimulus programme cushioned the downturn and recovery began by late 2009 as Asian demand recovered. The episode reinforced the structural vulnerability of Thailand's trade-dependent growth model.

title: Red Shirt Crackdown Kills 91 in Bangkok — Ratchaprasong Occupation
description: Red Shirt protesters occupied the Ratchaprasong commercial district in central Bangkok from April to May 2010, paralysing the capital's business heart. The military crackdown on 19 May 2010 left at least 91 people dead and nearly 2,000 injured, with the burning of Central World shopping centre. The violence deepened Thailand's political polarisation and entrenched perceptions of class-based injustice.

title: Yingluck Shinawatra Elected — First Female Prime Minister
description: Pheu Thai, led by Yingluck Shinawatra, Thaksin's younger sister, won a decisive election in July 2011 taking 265 of 500 seats. Yingluck became Thailand's first female prime minister, and her election was interpreted as a popular mandate overturning the judicial outcomes of 2008. The result reaffirmed that electoral politics in Thailand consistently favoured the Thaksin political network's rural base.

title: Catastrophic Floods Cause $46.5 Billion in Losses, Disrupt Global Supply Chains
description: The 2011 floods, worst in Thailand in fifty years, inundated large parts of central Thailand from July to December, affecting 13.6 million people and killing over 815. Major industrial estates in Ayutthaya and Pathum Thani hosting Japanese factories were submerged for weeks, disrupting global hard-drive and automotive supply chains. The World Bank estimated economic losses of US $46.5 billion.

title: PDRC Protests Paralyse Bangkok, Setting Stage for 2014 Coup
description: The People's Democratic Reform Committee mobilised massive anti-government protests in Bangkok from October 2013, following the collapse of Yingluck's amnesty bill. PDRC leader Suthep Thaugsuban demanded an appointed people's council to reform Thailand before new elections, effectively seeking a non-electoral transfer of power. The protests paralysed Bangkok for months and the Constitutional Court annulled the February 2014 snap election.

title: Prayuth Chan-ocha Stages Coup, Establishes NCPO Junta
description: Army Commander Prayuth Chan-ocha staged a coup on 22 May 2014, establishing the National Council for Peace and Order (NCPO), the twelfth coup since 1932. The junta suspended the constitution, declared martial law, arrested hundreds of politicians and activists, and granted Prayuth near-unlimited executive and legislative powers under Section 44 of an interim charter. Prayuth justified the seizure as necessary to end political violence and reform the country.

title: Erawan Shrine Bombing Kills 20 in Central Bangkok
description: A bomb exploded at the Erawan Hindu shrine in central Bangkok on 17 August 2015, killing 20 people and injuring more than 120 at a site popular with Chinese and Southeast Asian tourists. Thai authorities arrested suspects with Turkish passports linked to networks affected by Thai deportations of Uyghur migrants. The attack rattled the tourist industry and prompted enhanced security measures across tourist sites.

title: Military Charter Approved in Restricted Referendum with Appointed Senate
description: A referendum on the NCPO-drafted constitution passed with 61 percent support in August 2016, though campaigning against it had been criminalised and critics had been arrested. The approved constitution included a five-year fully appointed Senate with power to participate in prime ministerial selection. The charter institutionalised military oversight of elected governments through multiple unelected veto bodies.

title: King Bhumibol Dies After 70-Year Reign — Era of Stabilising Monarchy Ends
description: King Bhumibol Adulyadej, the world's longest-reigning monarch, died on 13 October 2016 aged 88 after prolonged illness. His 70-year reign had made him the uniquely stabilising and beloved centrepiece of Thai national identity, intervening decisively in political crises in 1973, 1981, and 1992. His death plunged Thailand into a year-long mourning period and raised profound questions about the monarchy's future political role.

title: King Vajiralongkorn Proclaimed Rama X, Amends Constitution for Royal Powers
description: Crown Prince Vajiralongkorn was officially proclaimed King Rama X on 1 December 2016 and requested amendments to the 2017 constitution giving the palace direct control over royal assets and expanded personal powers without a regent. The new king's assertive approach to constitutional arrangements differed markedly from his father's style. His royal cremation ceremony in October 2017 drew millions of mourning Thais to Bangkok.

title: Tham Luang Cave Rescue — International Operation Saves 13 Trapped
description: In June-July 2018, twelve boys and their football coach became trapped in the Tham Luang cave complex in Chiang Rai after monsoon flooding sealed the entrance. An international rescue operation involving expert divers from multiple countries successfully extracted all thirteen over three days beginning 8 July. The operation generated intense global attention and brought Thailand overwhelmingly positive international coverage.

title: Eastern Economic Corridor Launched to Attract High-Technology Investment
description: Thailand launched the Eastern Economic Corridor (EEC) in 2018 as a flagship initiative to attract foreign investment in advanced manufacturing, aerospace, and digital industries through tax incentives and streamlined regulation. The corridor built on the existing eastern seaboard industrial zones established in the 1980s. The EEC represented the junta's signature economic legacy project aimed at moving Thailand up global value chains.

title: Disputed Election Returns Prayuth Despite Opposition Popular Majority
description: General elections in March 2019 saw pro-democracy parties win more popular votes, but the electoral system and 250 appointed senators ensured Prayuth Chan-ocha was returned as prime minister. The Election Commission's delayed counting and party-seat allocation formulae were widely criticised. Future Forward Party's 81 seats made it an overnight opposition sensation before its dissolution the following year.

title: Future Forward Dissolved — Youth Protests Demand Monarchy Reform
description: The Constitutional Court dissolved the Future Forward Party in February 2020, ruling it had illegally received a loan from its leader. The dissolution triggered massive student-led protests making unprecedented demands for monarchy reform alongside democratic governance, including curbing royal prerogatives and amending the lèse-majesté law. The youth movement represented a new political generation breaking a long-standing taboo.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic Collapses Tourism, GDP Contracts 6.1 Percent
description: The COVID-19 pandemic devastated Thailand's economy in 2020, with GDP contracting approximately 6.1 percent as international tourism — roughly 12 percent of GDP — disappeared almost entirely from over 50 million arrivals in 2019 to near zero. The crisis exposed the structural risks of extreme dependence on tourism and prompted calls for economic diversification.

title: Lèse-Majesté Prosecutions Multiply — Over 200 Cases Against Activists
description: Thai authorities filed more than 200 lèse-majesté cases under Article 112 between 2020 and 2022 against protest leaders, activists, and students, with penalties of three to fifteen years per count. Many accused faced multiple simultaneous charges. Human rights organisations condemned the prosecutions as criminalisation of political speech, documenting Thailand among the world's most intensive users of monarchical defamation laws.

title: Move Forward Wins Election but Is Blocked from Government by Senate
description: Move Forward led by Pita Limjaroenrat won 151 seats in the May 2023 election, the most of any party, and formed an eight-party coalition commanding 313 seats. Pita was blocked from the premiership twice by the military-appointed Senate, which combined with elected members to deny the 376-vote threshold. Pheu Thai then abandoned the coalition, formed a government with pro-military parties, and elected real estate tycoon Srettha Thavisin prime minister.

title: Thaksin Returns from Exile After 15 Years, Begins Prison Term
description: Thaksin Shinawatra returned to Thailand on 22 August 2023 after fifteen years in self-imposed exile, landing at Don Mueang airport to considerable fanfare before being taken into custody to serve his corruption sentence, later reduced on medical grounds. His return coincided with Pheu Thai's entry into government, fuelling widespread allegations that a deal had been struck with conservative elites enabling his repatriation.

title: Move Forward Dissolved; Paetongtarn Shinawatra Becomes PM
description: The Constitutional Court dissolved the Move Forward Party in August 2024, ruling its campaign to amend the lèse-majesté law threatened the constitutional monarchy, and banned Pita Limjaroenrat from politics for ten years. Days later, the court removed Prime Minister Srettha on ethics grounds, and parliament elected Paetongtarn Shinawatra, Thaksin's youngest daughter, as Thailand's youngest premier. Move Forward reconstituted as the People's Party, perpetuating the cycle of party dissolution and reconstitution.
